study_identification.title: Atypical Brain Asymmetry in Autism -A Candidate for Clinically Meaningful Strati /uniFB01 cation

study_characteristics.study_objective: To dissect heterogeneity in lateralization in autism and to identify laterality-related subtypes by considering co-occurring clinical symptoms in autism such as language development.

quality_checking_detail.answer: Exclusion criteria included the presence of any MRI contraindications (e.g., metal implants, braces, claustrophobia) or failure to give informed written consent to MRI scanning, as well as significant hearing or visual impairments not corrected by glasses or hearing aids. In addition, we excluded participants with missing T1-weighted MRI scans, low image quality (i.e., structural brain abnormality, excessive head motion, insufficient coverage), and failed image preprocessing. Due to low number of participants from the Rome site after quality control, we restricted analyses to the five remaining sites. Neurotypical controls scoring positively for attention-deficit hyper-activity disorder (ADHD) as assessed by the DSM-5 ADHD rating scale were also excluded.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: We trained a Gaussian process regression model at each voxel on the neurotypical cohort using age, sex, and site as covariates to predict gray matter asymmetry. We also ran a control analysis using ComBat.

predictor_effects.answer: Age, sex, and site were used as covariates.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The normative model included age, sex, and site as covariates to account for nuisance variables. A control analysis using ComBat for site effect removal was also performed.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: First, we trained a Gaussian process regression model at each voxel on the neurotypical cohort using age, sex, and site as covariates to predict gray matter asymmetry, resulting in a developmental model of gray matter asymmetry in neurotypical individuals... To assess robustness, we conducted a set of control analyses. 1) We estimated a separate normative model without including site as a covariate, but removing site effects using ComBat (57).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: 10-fold cross-validation was used in the neurotypical cohort to assess the generalizability of the model.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To avoid over /uniFB01 tting, assess generalizability, and determine whether neurotypical individuals fall within the normative range, we used 10-fold cross-validation in neurotypical individuals before retraining the model in the entire sample to make predictions in individuals with autism.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not use an independent dataset from the same domain for validation.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The model was replicated on the ABIDE I and II datasets.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To assess replicability, we selected a sample from the publicly available Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) I and II (59,60) to examine extreme rightand leftward deviations in an independent dataset.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Relative importance analyses, Pearson's correlations, and general linear models were used to examine associations between deviation scores and clinical variables (language delay, ADHD, handedness, sex, and symptom severity).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Individuals with autism showed highly individualized patterns of both extreme right- and leftward deviations from the normative pattern of brain laterality, which were associated with symptom severity and language delay.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study found that individuals with autism have unique patterns of brain asymmetry deviations. Extreme rightward deviations were linked to language delay, while extreme leftward deviations were associated with core autism symptom severity. A stepwise pattern emerged, with individuals with autism and language delay showing the most pronounced rightward deviations. These findings were replicated in the ABIDE dataset.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The sample size of subgroups decreased substantially when dividing by diagnostic group, sex, LD, and site. Residual site effects cannot be fully excluded. The study did not investigate experience-dependent influences on cortical asymmetry. The approach might be less sensitive to reduced laterality (i.e., lack of specialization).
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The authors suggest that atypical lateralization may be a useful neurophenotype for clinically meaningful stratification in autism, which could have implications for early prognosis and individualized interventions.

general_notes.general_notes: The study used a normative modeling approach to move beyond traditional case-control comparisons and examine individual-level differences in brain asymmetry. The results highlight the heterogeneity of autism and the potential of using neurobiological markers for stratification.
